title: Fungi: budding and spores
subtitle: How was the new fungal cell formed?
subject: Biology
lessonIntent: Explain named budding and spore pathways and classify them from formation evidence.
examSkill: Use mechanism evidence rather than the word spore.

scenes.heading: A spore does not tell the whole story

bullets.text: Spore = a cell that can start new fungal growth.
Ask how the spore was formed.

scenes.caption: A spore does not tell the whole story

voiceover.text: Imagine finding a fungal spore on a surface. Can you tell whether it came from sexual or asexual reproduction? The spore alone does not settle that question. Fungi can produce spores through either pathway. We need to know how it was formed. Today we will use two named examples to explain that difference: budding in baker's yeast, and asexual spores in bread mould. Then we will connect yeast spores to a sexual cycle.

scenes.heading: A bud becomes another yeast cell
scenes.caption: A bud becomes another yeast cell

voiceover.text: Baker's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, is a single-celled fungus. In budding, a small outgrowth develops on the parent cell. The cell copies its DNA, the information it passes on. Its nucleus, the compartment containing that DNA, divides by mitosis. Mitosis separates copied genetic information into two nuclei. One nucleus enters the growing bud. The bud can then separate as a daughter cell. This event is asexual because no reproductive cells or nuclei fuse. Copying supports similar inherited information, although mutations, changes in DNA, can still occur.

scenes.heading: Bread mould can make asexual spores
scenes.caption: Bread mould can make asexual spores

voiceover.text: Now consider the asexual pathway of bread mould, Rhizopus stolonifer. Its body includes hyphae: thin growing threads. A sporangium is a spore-containing structure at the tip of a specialised stalk. In this pathway, spores form through mitosis without fusion. Releasing them allows dispersal, movement away from the parent fungus. A spore that reaches suitable conditions can germinate, meaning it begins to grow. It produces hyphae that develop into a new fungal body. Dispersal creates opportunities, but landing somewhere does not guarantee growth. The spore still needs suitable moisture, nutrients and other conditions.

scenes.heading: Yeast also has a sexual pathway

bullets.text: This is a simplified named model.

scenes.caption: Yeast also has a sexual pathway

voiceover.text: The same yeast species has another pathway. In a simplified baker's yeast model, compatible cells of different mating types can join. Their nuclei then fuse, bringing chromosome sets together. A chromosome is a DNA-containing structure. A haploid cell has one set of chromosomes; a diploid cell has two. Nuclear fusion produces a diploid cell. This is part of sexual reproduction. Compatibility matters: simply putting any two yeast cells together does not establish that fusion will occur. Fungi do not all use the sperm-and-egg arrangement we met in animals and flowering plants.

scenes.heading: Spores can belong to a sexual cycle

bullets.text: This named cell has two chromosome sets.

scenes.caption: Spores can belong to a sexual cycle

voiceover.text: Under suitable nutrient-limiting conditions, a diploid baker's yeast cell can undergo meiosis and form spores. Meiosis is a cell division that reduces two chromosome sets to one and can reshuffle inherited information. The resulting haploid nuclei are packaged into spores. This spore formation belongs to the sexual life cycle we have just traced: fusion brought sets together, and meiosis separates them again. It is different from the mitotic spores in our bread-mould example. So the word spore describes a reproductive cell, not a guarantee that the pathway was asexual. These are selected examples, not a rule that all fungi have the same life cycle.

scenes.heading: Try these two cases

bullets.text: A: bread mould. Mitosis forms spores; no fusion.
B: yeast. Cells and nuclei fuse; meiosis forms spores.
Classify each pathway as sexual or asexual. Give formation evidence.
Explain why spore alone is insufficient.

scenes.caption: Try these two cases

voiceover.text: Case A: a bread-mould culture produces spores by mitosis, with no fusion. Case B: compatible yeast cells and their nuclei fuse, and a diploid cell later forms spores through meiosis. Classify each supplied pathway as sexual or asexual, and give the evidence for your choice. Why would the word spore alone be insufficient? Pause here if you want more thinking time.

scenes.callout: Think quietly. Pause for more time.

bullets.text: A is asexual: mitosis without fusion.
B traces a sexual cycle: fusion, then meiosis.
Both produce spores. Their formation differs.

voiceover.text: Case A is asexual. The supplied mitosis-and-no-fusion evidence explains that classification. Case B traces a sexual pathway: compatible cells and nuclei fuse, followed later by meiosis and spore formation. Both cases end with spores, but they reach that result differently. If you classified both as asexual just because spores were named, return to the events that produced them. No observation about the final shape can replace that pathway evidence.

bullets.text: How was the new cell formed?
Next: bacterial division and DNA exchange.

voiceover.text: When you meet a fungal reproductive event, ask how the new cell was formed. Budding in our yeast example grows a daughter cell without fusion. Our bread-mould example makes mitotic spores. Yeast can also form spores within a sexual cycle involving nuclear fusion and meiosis. Keep those examples scoped to their organisms and supplied conditions. Next we will consider bacteria, where cell division and exchanges of DNA need to be distinguished. You can pause the optional notes screen to record the essentials.

scenes.heading: Key notes
points: Yeast budding is asexual, without fusion.
Rhizopus can form asexual spores by mitosis.
A sexual yeast cycle includes nuclear fusion and meiosis.
A spore alone does not identify the pathway.
